title: How to Find Real Estate Syndication Deals to Invest In (Step-by-Step Guide)
excerpt: Real estate syndication lets you invest in large properties without managing them yourself — but finding the right deals takes strategy. This guide breaks down exactly where to look, what to evaluate, and how to get started with your first syndication investment.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: how to find real estate syndication deals to invest in
metaDescription: Learn how to find real estate syndication deals to invest in with this step-by-step guide covering networks, platforms, due diligence, and key metrics.

sections.content: Real estate syndication is one of the most powerful ways to build wealth passively. Instead of buying a $3 million apartment complex by yourself, you pool money with other investors. A sponsor — often called the syndicator or general partner — finds the deal, manages the property, and handles the day-to-day. You invest as a limited partner and collect returns. Simple in theory, but finding quality syndication deals to invest in takes real effort and the right connections. This guide walks you through exactly how to do it.
What Is a Real Estate Syndication Deal?

A real estate syndication is a group investment where multiple investors fund the purchase of a large asset — typically an apartment building, commercial property, or storage facility. The general partner (GP) sources the deal, secures financing, and operates the property. Limited partners (LPs) contribute capital and receive a share of cash flow and profits at sale. A typical structure might offer LPs an 8% preferred return plus 70% of profits above that threshold. Syndications often require a minimum investment between $25,000 and $100,000, making them accessible to accredited investors who want real estate exposure without landlord headaches. If you're newer to investing broadly, our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide is a great foundation before diving into syndications.
Step 1 — Build Your Network First

The uncomfortable truth about syndication deals is that most of the best ones never get publicly advertised. They're filled through the sponsor's personal network before a public offering ever happens. This means your number one job as a passive investor is to build relationships with active syndicators. Start attending local real estate investor meetups, BiggerPockets events, and national conferences like Best Ever Conference or IMN. Follow multifamily syndicators on LinkedIn and engage meaningfully with their content. The goal is simple: get on their investor list before the next deal closes.
Pro Tip: Tell every syndicator you meet exactly what you're looking for — asset class, market, minimum returns, hold period. Specific investors get called first. Vague ones get forgotten.
Step 2 — Use Online Syndication Platforms

Technology has opened the syndication world to more investors than ever. Several platforms now aggregate deals from vetted sponsors and allow you to review offerings, financials, and track records in one place. Some of the most active platforms include CrowdStreet, RealtyMogul, EquityMultiple, and Fundrise. Each platform has different minimums, vetting standards, and asset types. CrowdStreet, for example, focuses on commercial real estate and typically requires accredited investor status with minimums starting at $25,000. RealtyMogul offers both accredited and non-accredited options. Spend time comparing at least three platforms before committing capital anywhere.

items: CrowdStreet — Commercial and multifamily deals, accredited investors, $25K+ minimums
RealtyMogul — Mixed offerings for accredited and non-accredited investors
EquityMultiple — Focus on institutional-quality commercial deals
Fundrise — Lower minimums ($10), eREIT structure, great for beginners
Yieldstreet — Alternative assets including real estate debt and equity deals

sections.content: Step 3 — Connect With Active Sponsors Directly

Beyond platforms, many of the strongest syndication opportunities come directly from individual operators who raise capital outside of third-party portals. Search for sponsors who specialize in markets you believe in. High-growth metros like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) have been particularly active in multifamily syndications over the past decade due to strong population growth and job creation. Reach out to operators who own assets in those markets, ask for their investor deck, and request to join their private email list. Most operators send deal summaries to their list before going public.

'Your net worth is directly tied to your network. The best syndication deals don't find passive investors — passive investors find the best operators.' — Common wisdom in the real estate investment community
Step 4 — Evaluate the Deal Like a Pro
Once you start receiving deal offerings, you need a framework to evaluate them quickly and accurately. Don't get distracted by flashy projected returns. Focus on the fundamentals of the deal itself.
Key Metrics to Review in Any Syndication Offering

items: Cash-on-Cash Return: Look for 6–10% annually in stable markets. Anything above 12% projected deserves extra scrutiny.
Internal Rate of Return (IRR): A healthy deal typically projects 14–20% IRR over a 3–7 year hold period.
Equity Multiple: A 1.8x–2.2x equity multiple means you'd turn $50,000 into $90,000–$110,000 over the hold.
Preferred Return: Most deals offer an 8% pref before the GP shares profits. Know what's guaranteed vs. projected.
Debt Structure: Fixed-rate, long-term debt is far safer than floating-rate bridge loans in a high-rate environment.
Sponsor Track Record: How many deals have they exited? What were actual vs. projected returns? Ask for references.

sections.content: Pro Tip: Always model a stress scenario. If occupancy drops to 80% and rents fall 10%, does the deal still service its debt? If the answer isn't clear in the offering memorandum, ask the sponsor directly. Their response tells you a lot.
Step 5 — Verify the Market and the Asset

Great operators invest in great markets. Before you invest in any syndication, independently research the local market conditions — job growth, population trends, new supply coming online, and rent growth history. If a sponsor tells you rents are growing at 5% annually in a submarket, verify that claim with third-party sources like CoStar, Apartment List, or local brokerage reports. Also request a third-party property inspection report and an independent appraisal if possible. You're trusting a team with your capital for 5+ years — do the homework that protects your investment.

It also helps to understand how syndicators analyze deals on the acquisition side. If you're curious about how sponsors evaluate wholesale and off-market properties before packaging them into a syndication, tools like the [Deal Calculator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) can help you understand how investors underwrite potential acquisitions and estimate profitability before committing capital. Understanding the operator's perspective makes you a sharper passive investor. And if you want to go deeper on the sourcing side of the business, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide explains how deals get found and structured before they reach investors.
Step 6 — Understand the Legal Structure Before You Sign

Every syndication deal comes with a Private Placement Memorandum (PPM) — a legal document that outlines the full terms of the investment. Read it carefully or hire a real estate attorney to review it for you. Key sections to understand include the waterfall structure (how profits are divided), the preferred return terms, any clawback provisions, the sponsor's fee structure (acquisition fees typically run 1–2% of purchase price), and exit strategy triggers. Most syndications are structured as LLCs or LPs, and your rights as a limited partner are defined entirely by this document. Never skip this step.
Common Sponsor Fees to Watch For

items: Acquisition Fee: 1–3% of the purchase price, paid at closing
Asset Management Fee: 1–2% of gross revenue annually
Disposition Fee: 1–2% of the sale price when the property sells
Construction Management Fee: 5–10% of renovation costs if heavy value-add is involved
Refinance Fee: Some sponsors charge a fee when the property is refinanced

sections.content: Reasonable fees are normal and expected — sponsors work hard to find and manage deals. But stacked fee structures that pay the GP regardless of performance should raise flags. Look for alignment: sponsors who co-invest their own capital alongside LPs tend to be more careful stewards of the deal.
Where to Find Syndication Deals Summary

items: Attend real estate conferences and local investor meetups to meet syndicators in person
Join platforms like CrowdStreet, RealtyMogul, EquityMultiple, and Fundrise
Connect directly with operators active in growth markets like Atlanta, Dallas, and Phoenix
Subscribe to syndication newsletters and podcasts (Passive Pockets, Multifamily Investor Nation)
Join Facebook groups and LinkedIn communities focused on passive real estate investing
Ask your CPA, financial advisor, or attorney for referrals to syndicators they know and trust
